turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, thank you for seeing me. It’s just… well, what brings me in is that I feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. And I mean *constantly*. 

I teach special education—I’ve been doing it a long time, and you'd think at 58 years old I'd be looking forward to winding down a bit, maybe taking things at a slower pace, right? But it's the exact opposite. I finish one thing at school, maybe I'm working with a student on a reading assignment or setting up an activity, and the second that's done, boom, I immediately jump into the next thing. I don't even take a breath. I'm just going and going and going. 

And then the bell rings, I drive home, and you'd think I'd sit down in a chair for five minutes to decompress, but no. I walk through the front door and immediately start fixing a squeaky hinge on a cabinet, or I'm out in the yard pulling weeds, or I'm just moving around the house looking for the next task. I just... I can't ever seem to shut myself off. It’s like someone flipped a switch inside me to "on" and then just broke the lever right off, so I'm stuck at top speed all day long. It's honestly exhausting just never, ever being able to stop and just *be*.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states feeling like they are 'constantly running on a motor' and are unable to stop moving from one task to the next without taking a break.

turns.doctor_question: During these periods when you feel like you’re running on a motor, do you also feel unusually upbeat or euphoric?
turns.patient_response:
Euphoric? Oh, gosh, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, don't get me wrong, I like my job, most days anyway. Working with those kids, it has its moments of joy, of course. Like last Tuesday when one of my boys finally grasped this phonics concept we've been drilling for weeks, that felt great. But this... this motor feeling? It's not a happy, on-top-of-the-world kind of energy. 

It's not like I'm walking on sunshine or feeling invincible or anything like that. It's actually kind of the opposite, emotionally speaking. It's more of a relentless pressure. Like I just have to keep moving. I'm not doing all these things, you know, fixing the cabinet, pulling the weeds, running from task to task at school, because I'm just in this fantastic, upbeat mood and want to take on the world. I'm doing them because if I sit still, I feel like I'm going to crawl out of my skin. 

It's a very mechanical feeling, if that makes sense? Just gears grinding and pushing me forward. So, no, definitely not euphoric. If anything, I'm just incredibly frustrated by it, because I want to relax, I really do. My wife will even ask me to just sit down and watch the evening news with her, and I want to, but my body just won't let me. So there is no euphoria there, just exhaustion and this endless, annoying need to be doing something.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had trouble with attention, distractibility, or feeling restless since you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, actually. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my older sister about this the other day, and she reminded me of how I was when I was a kid. It definitely isn't a new thing, not by a long shot. I mean, my mother—bless her heart, she passed away about ten years ago—she used to have this running joke about me when I was in elementary school. I think it started around second or third grade, maybe earlier, but she used to tell everyone that I taught the class from my seat. 

And she didn't mean it as a compliment about my intelligence, she meant it because I literally could not stay in my chair. I was always up, always moving around, always talking. My teachers would be in the middle of giving directions for a math worksheet or explaining a spelling rule, and I’d just blurt out the answer or cut right in before they even finished their sentence. I just didn't have that filter, that ability to wait my turn or just sit quietly and listen. 

So, yes, this restlessness, this inability to just stop and focus without feeling like I need to be doing ten other things... it's been a part of who I am for as long as I can remember. Long before I became an adult, long before I started teaching, long before any of the recent stresses or family changes I've had. It's just... it's always been there, humming away in the background. It’s just that lately, it feels like it’s gotten completely out of hand, you know? Like it’s dialed up to eleven all the time now. But the foundation of it? Oh yeah, that goes way, way back to when I was just a little boy in short pants, driving my poor teachers crazy.
